marble.name: Using a Microscope
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Use a light microscope correctly to prepare, focus, and examine biological specimens, including making accurate labelled drawings at an appropriate magnification
marble.prompt: If you had to use a school microscope to study a biological specimen, could they set it up correctly, find what they're looking for, and produce a labelled scientific drawing of what they see?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about the amazing diversity of life — identifying different animals and plants, understanding how body parts help animals survive, and discovering what all living things need to stay alive.

misconceptions: Dropping the coverslip flat and then reading the resulting air bubble as a cell.
Using the coarse focus on high power and driving the objective into (and cracking) the slide.
Starting on the highest magnification rather than the lowest to locate the specimen first.
Thinking magnification is just the objective value, forgetting to multiply by the eyepiece.
Shading or 'artistic' drawings instead of clear labelled line drawings with a scale.
representations: A labelled light microscope (eyepiece, objectives, stage, coarse/fine focus, light source)
A focusing sequence (blurred → sharp) showing coarse-then-fine on low power
A magnification calculation (eyepiece × objective; image ÷ actual size)
A labelled biological drawing with a scale bar as the recorded output
authoredAnswer: The student makes a bubble-free wet mount, starts on the lowest-power objective, uses coarse focus while watching from the side to avoid driving the lens into the slide, then fine focus, centres the specimen before increasing magnification, draws only what is actually seen with a scale, and calculates total magnification as eyepiece × objective.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Drives the objective down onto the slide, risking cracking it, and can't find focus
wrongAnswers.fix: Lower the lens while watching from the side, then focus by moving it UP and away from the slide. Model it once, then let them redo.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Begins on the high-power objective and cannot locate anything in the field
wrongAnswers.fix: Always start on the lowest objective to find and centre the specimen, then step up the magnification.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Reports 40× when using a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective, instead of 400×
wrongAnswers.fix: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective; work through the multiplication with the actual lenses in use.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Produces an idealised diagram (or omits bubbles/folds) that doesn't match the slide
wrongAnswers.fix: A biological drawing records observation, not memory; draw exactly what is seen, artefacts and all. Scaffold, don't reteach the concept.

before.name: Cells Under the Microscope
before.reason: Microscope technique is learned in the context of observing cells
